# Reflections

I learnt how to visualise data distributions using ridgeline and raincloud plots in R. This exercise showed me how these plots can compare groups more clearly by showing spread, patterns, clusters, and differences in scores beyond a normal boxplot.

# Getting started

## Installing and loading packages

The R packages that will be used are as follow:

-   **ggridges**: a ggplot2 extension specially designed for plotting ridgeline plots,

-   **ggdist**: a ggplot2 extension specially design for visualising distribution and uncertainty,

-   **tidyverse**: a family of R packages to meet the modern data science and visual communication needs,

-   **ggthemes**: a ggplot extension that provides the user additional themes, scales, and geoms for the ggplots package, and

-   **colorspace**: an R package provides a broad toolbox for selecting individual colors or color palettes, manipulating these colors, and employing them in various kinds of visualisations.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(ggdist, ggridges, ggthemes,
               colorspace, tidyverse)
```
:::


## Data importing

We will be using Exam_data.csv for this exercise. The read_csv() used in previous exercise is used to import


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
exam <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")
```
:::


# Visualising Distribution with Ridgeline Plot

Understanding what is ridgeline plot: [*Ridgeline plot*](https://www.data-to-viz.com/graph/ridgeline.html) (sometimes called *Joyplot*) is a data visualisation technique for revealing the distribution of a numeric value for several groups. Distribution can be represented using histograms or density plots, all aligned to the same horizontal scale and presented with a slight overlap.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = "grey70",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "ENGLISH",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = "CLASS", 
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))
  ) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Ridgeline plots make sense when the number of group to represent is medium to high, and thus a classic window separation would take to much space. Groups overlap each other allows to use space more efficiently. If you have less than 5 groups, dealing with other distribution plots is probably better.

It works well when there is a clear pattern in the result, like if there is an obvious ranking in groups. Otherwise group will tend to overlap each other, leading to a messy plot not providing any insight.

## Plotting ridgeline graph: ggridges method

There are different ways to plot ridgeline plot with R. Here we will learn how to plot using [ggridges](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/index.html) package

ggridges package provides two main geom to plot gridgeline plots, they are: [`geom_ridgeline()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_ridgeline.html) and [`geom_density_ridges()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_density_ridges.html). The former takes height values directly to draw the ridgelines, and the latter first estimates data densities and then draws those using ridgelines.

Below shows ridgeline plot using geom_density_ridges()

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

## Varying fill colors along the x axis

We can also create area under a ridgeline with varying colors. This can be achieved by either [`geom_ridgeline_gradient()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_ridgeline_gradient.html) or [`geom_density_ridges_gradient()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_ridgeline_gradient.html). Both geoms work just like `geom_ridgeline()` and `geom_density_ridges()`, except that they allow for varying fill colors. However, they do not allow for alpha transparency in the fill. For technical reasons, we can have changing fill colors or transparency but not both.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "English score",
                       option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges() 
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Temp. [F]",
                       option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges() 
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

## Mapping the probabilities directly onto colour

Beside providing additional geom objects to support the need to plot ridgeline plot, ggridges package also provides a stat function called [`stat_density_ridges()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/stat_density_ridges.html) that replaces [`stat_density()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html) of ggplot2.

Figure below is plotted by mapping the probabilities calculated by using `stat(ecdf)` which represent the empirical cumulative density function for the distribution of English score.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()         
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()        
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

**NOTE:** It is important include the argument `calc_ecdf = TRUE` in `stat_density_ridges()`.

## Ridgeline plots with quantile lines

We can even color the ridgeline plot by quantile by using geom_density_ridges_gradient() via the calculated stat(quantile) aesthetic as shown in the figure below

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()       
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()      
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

Instead of using number to define the quantiles, we can also specify quantiles by cut points such as 2.5% and 97.5% tails to colour the ridgeline plot as shown in the figure below.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)
    ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)
    ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::

# Visualising Distribution with Raincloud Plot

A raincloud plot is used to show the distribution of data in more detail than a normal boxplot. It combines density, boxplot, and data points, making it easier to see where values are clustered and whether there are different groups or patterns in the data.

We will learn how to create a raincloud plot below to visualise the distribution of English score by race. It will be created by using functions provided by ggdist and ggplot2 packages.

## Plotting a half eye graph

First, we will plot a Half-Eye graph by using [`stat_halfeye()`](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/reference/stat_halfeye.html) of **ggdist** package.

This produces a Half Eye visualisation, which contains a half-density and a slab interval.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

**\
Things to learn from the code chunk above**

We remove the slab interval by setting .width = 0 and point_colour = NA.

## Adding the boxplot with geom_boxplot()

Next, we will add the second geometry layer using [`geom_boxplot()`](https://r4va.netlify.app/chap09) of ggplot2. This produces a narrow boxplot. We reduce the width and adjust the opacity.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

## Adding the Dot Plots with stat_dots()

Next, we will add the third geometry layer using [`stat_dots()`](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/reference/stat_dots.html) of ggdist package. This produces a half-dotplot, which is similar to a histogram that indicates the number of samples (number of dots) in each bin. We select side = “left” to indicate we want it on the left-hand side.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

## Finishing touch

Lastly, [`coord_flip()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_flip.html) of ggplot2 package will be used to flip the raincloud chart horizontally to give it the raincloud appearance. At the same time, `theme_economist()` of ggthemes package is used to give the raincloud chart a professional publishing standard look.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex04a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::
